source: Pearson & Kosslyn (2015) The heterogeneity of mental representation: ending the imagery debate
finding: Authors argue the debate is settled: humans use at least two formats, propositional and depictive. Depictive means parts of the representation map to parts of the object, with distance preserved in a functional space.
numbers: Cites V1 decoding trained on perception that transfers to imagery; a Gabor-wavelet encoding model (Naselaris 2015) predicts which pictures are imagined; rTMS to medial occipital cortex impaired imagery and perception to a similar extent (Kosslyn 1999). No effect sizes given in the review.
limits: Written by a leading depictivist, so it is advocacy. Critics in the Pylyshyn line do not accept that V1 activity shows a functional picture. The rival side is not engaged in depth.
agent_relevance: Defines the format question cleanly: the same content can be held in different formats. O6 (change representation) rests on this claim.
quote: The debate was not about whether visual information is stored; it was about how.

source: Pearson & Kosslyn (2015) The heterogeneity of mental representation: ending the imagery debate (functional roles)
finding: Four proposed reasons for a depictive format: wiring economy, the principle of least commitment (images keep implicit information), mental simulation of interactions, and bridging language to perception.
numbers: Example given: asked the shape of a cat's ears, most people report visualizing. Packing a car trunk is the simulation example.
limits: The functional claims are argued, not measured, in this review.
agent_relevance: Least commitment is the best argument for O6: a grid keeps facts nobody wrote down; a text summary drops them.

source: Pearson & Kosslyn (2015) The heterogeneity of mental representation: ending the imagery debate (behavioral tuning)
finding: Imagery of a pattern biases later binocular rivalry in an orientation-specific, graded way, like perception (Pearson, Clifford, Tong 2008).
numbers: Peak bias when imagined and rivalry orientations match; smooth fall-off across orientation space. Exact effect sizes not given in the review.
limits: Rivalry priming is also the measure that is weak in aphantasia (see b16), so it tracks vividness, not format alone.
agent_relevance: An imagery effect that a purely descriptive code would not obviously predict to be graded.

source: Pylyshyn (1973, 2002, 2003) What the mind's eye tells the mind's brain; Mental imagery: in search of a theory; Return of the mental image
finding: Critique: scanning and rotation effects can come from tacit knowledge of how the real world behaves plus propositional structures. Image experience is epiphenomenal. The 1973 paper is dated as the start of the debate by Pearson and Kosslyn.
numbers: No numbers. Recalled from memory of the BBS target article; not opened this session.
limits: Not opened. Treat details as unverified.
agent_relevance: Strongest counter to O6: if the model already holds a relational description, a drawn grid may add nothing. Test it, do not assume it.

source: Kosslyn (1973) Scanning visual images: some structural implications
finding: Time to scan between points on a remembered image grows with distance. Read as evidence for a space-like format. Cited in Pearson and Kosslyn.
numbers: Response time rises with scan distance; slopes not checked.
limits: Not opened. Demand-characteristics and tacit-knowledge accounts later challenged the reading.
agent_relevance: Distance-sensitive cost is a signature to look for in a model's own spatial trace.

source: Shepard & Metzler (1971) Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects
finding: Time to judge whether two 3D shapes match grows with the angle between them, as if one is rotated. Cited in Pearson and Kosslyn.
numbers: Described as response time rising with rotation angle; numbers not checked.
limits: Not opened. Pearson and Kosslyn say response-time data alone were too unconstraining.
agent_relevance: Source of the 'rotate it mentally' operation that LLM spatial work imitates.

source: Kosslyn et al. (1999) The role of area 17 in visual imagery: PET and rTMS
finding: rTMS over medial occipital cortex impaired imagery and perception to a similar degree, as summarized by Pearson and Kosslyn.
numbers: Paper not opened; magnitude not recorded.
limits: Single-lab result as cited; not checked for later replication.
agent_relevance: Supports a depictive code in humans only. Says nothing about transformers.

source: Jolicoeur & Kosslyn (1985) Is time to scan visual images due to demand characteristics?
finding: Reported (as recalled) that the scan-time effect persists when participants are naive about the aim. Offered as the reply to the tacit-knowledge critique.
numbers: From memory; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened; unverified. Intons-Peterson (1983) found that experimenter expectations could shift imagery effects; the two are not reconciled here.
agent_relevance: A prompt can plant the effect it then finds. Hide the expected answer when testing visualization prompts.

source: Intons-Peterson (1983) Imagery paradigms: how vulnerable are they to experimenters' expectations?
finding: Imagery effects varied with what experimenters were led to expect. Used by the descriptive side as a demand-characteristics argument.
numbers: From memory; no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened; unverified.
agent_relevance: Our evals should hide the hypothesis from prompt writer and grader.

source: Bainbridge et al. (2021) Quantifying aphantasia through drawing: those without visual imagery show deficits in object but not spatial memory
finding: People with aphantasia recall fewer objects but place them as accurately as controls. Object detail and spatial layout dissociate.
numbers: 61 aphantasic (VVIQ <=25) vs 52 controls (VVIQ >=40); 2,795 online scorers. Share of objects drawn from memory: 0.261 (SD 0.165) vs 0.369 (SD 0.162), Z=4.09, r=0.39, p=4.2e-5. Location error under 10% of image size in both groups.
limits: Self-selected online sample; aphantasic group older (41.9 vs 32.1 years). Drawing is a reconstruction task, not a direct test of format.
agent_relevance: Supports a split between object content and spatial layout. An agent may need a layout code (grid) kept separate from object description.

source: Bainbridge et al. (2021) (questionnaire dissociation)
finding: Object-imagery self-report differs hugely between groups; spatial-imagery self-report does not.
numbers: OSIQ total: t(103)=12.70, d=2.48. Object subscale t(103)=20.00, d=3.80; spatial subscale t(103)=-0.33, p=0.742.
limits: Groups were selected on VVIQ, which is object-heavy, so the object gap is partly built in by selection.
agent_relevance: The object/spatial split is the best human analogue of pictorial vs symbolic coding that holds up.

source: Bainbridge et al. (2021) (verbal scaffolding and perception control)
finding: Aphantasic participants leaned on words in their drawings and made fewer memory errors. No group difference when copying the images in view.
numbers: Differences appeared only at recall, not in the matched perceptual copy. Text labels did not change aphantasic object count (t(174)=0.07, p=0.947). Both groups recalled all three images (2.89 vs 2.92 of 3).
limits: Fewer errors could reflect a cautious style rather than a better code.
agent_relevance: A symbolic-only memory may hold less but invent less. Relevant to guardrails on invented detail.

source: Milton et al. (2021) Behavioral and neural signatures of visual imagery vividness extremes: aphantasia versus hyperphantasia
finding: Aphantasia, midrange and hyperphantasia groups differ in autobiographical memory and imagination but not in standard memory tests. Resting connectivity between prefrontal and visual network was stronger in hyperphantasia.
numbers: n=24 aphantasia, 25 hyperphantasia, 20 controls. VVIQ means 16.92, 56.95, 77.08. Prosopagnosia Index 55.71 vs 43.30 vs 38.72; F(2,66)=12.83, partial eta2=0.28.
limits: Mental rotation (Manikins) and curved-segments tests hit ceiling (over 90% and over 98% correct in all groups), so they could not separate groups. Famous-face test also at ceiling.
agent_relevance: People who report no images still solve rotation-type tasks. Imagery experience is not required for spatial task success, so a text-only route can work.

source: Thorudottir et al. (2020) The architect who lost the ability to imagine
finding: Acquired aphantasia in one architect after bilateral PCA stroke. Lesions overlapped heavily with other patients; the selective area was a small left fusiform patch and part of right lingual gyrus.
numbers: Single case (PL518) compared with 3 bilateral PCA patients and one right-lesion architect.
limits: One case; lesion inference is weak.
agent_relevance: Dissociation evidence: imagery can be lost while much of cognition stays. Not decisive for format.

source: Jacobs et al. (2018), as cited in Bainbridge 2021: single aphantasic participant
finding: One aphantasic participant matched controls on an imagery task and its working-memory twin, except at the hardest level.
numbers: N=1; no further numbers in the citing text.
limits: Seen only through citation; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Task success without images is possible, but the hardest cases may expose the missing code.

source: Keogh & Pearson (2018) The blind mind: no sensory visual imagery in aphantasia
finding: Aphantasic people show far weaker imagery-based priming in binocular rivalry, an objective sign that matches self-report. Described in Bainbridge 2021 text.
numbers: Seen only via citation; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. A 2024 follow-up title ('Revisiting the blind mind') was seen in a search listing only.
agent_relevance: An objective check of a self-report. Our agent has no report to trust, so it needs outcome checks.

source: Zeman et al. (2015) Lives without imagery: congenital aphantasia
finding: First naming and description of lifelong absence of visual imagery in otherwise high-functioning people.
numbers: Not opened; sample size not recorded.
limits: Self-selected, self-reported sample.
agent_relevance: Existence proof that spatial and verbal solutions can stand in for images.

source: Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2026) Mental image vividness and aphantasia judgements are fundamentally compromised by overlooked confounds
finding: Argues vividness ratings and aphantasia labels cannot be validated because the 'axis' separating an image from non-image thought is undefined. Group differences may be criterion confounds.
numbers: Argument paper; no new sample. Received 2025-02-10, accepted 2026-04-24.
limits: One position paper; author names not captured in the extracted text. Opposed by objective-marker work such as rivalry priming.
agent_relevance: A self-report of 'seeing' is weak evidence for format. Do not count the agent's own 'I visualized it' as evidence (G2).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Is a picture worth a thousand words? Delving into spatial reasoning for vision-language models (SpatialEval)
finding: On map, maze and grid tasks, vision-language models given only the image often score near or below chance. They rarely beat their own text backbone. With text and image together they lean on the text.
numbers: Three input formats (text-only, vision-only, vision+text) on Spatial-Map, Maze-Nav, Spatial-Grid. Some models fall below random guessing on vision-only. VLMs often beat their LLM counterparts on text-only input. Per-model percentages are in figures and not recorded here.
limits: Simple grid and map tasks; 2024-era models.
agent_relevance: Evidence against the idea that a picture beats a good text description. Default O6 target should be text with coordinates.

source: Fu et al. (2024) IsoBench: benchmarking multimodal foundation models on isomorphic representations
finding: Same problem presented as image or as text: models do worse with the image. Consistent preference for text.
numbers: 1,887 samples (math, science, algorithms, chess). Image worse than text by 28.7 points (Claude-3 Opus), 18.7 (GPT-4 Turbo), 14.9 (Gemini Pro).
limits: Images are rendered plots and diagrams; 2024-era models.
agent_relevance: For LLMs the symbolic form beats the pictorial form on equal content. Switch form only when the text form fails.

source: Fu et al. (2024) IsoBench (prompting remedies)
finding: Combining representations (IsoCombination) and translating the image to text first (IsoScratchPad) recover part of the gap.
numbers: IsoCB up to +9.4 points on graph algorithms over the best single representation; IsoSP up to +14.4 points on science problems.
limits: Best-case gains per domain, not averages.
agent_relevance: Translating picture to symbols is a cheap O6 move; showing both forms helps on graphs.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought elicits spatial reasoning in large language models
finding: Asking GPT-4 to draw a text grid of its state after each step beats plain chain of thought and a no-visualization version.
numbers: Natural-language navigation: VoT 59.00 vs CoT 54.00 vs no-viz 35.50 (VoT +23.5 over no-viz; p<0.16 vs CoT). Visual tiling: VoT 63.94 vs CoT 54.15 vs no-viz 46.98 vs GPT-4V CoT 49.62. Other task cells not read reliably from the extracted table.
limits: Small gains over CoT; model far from perfect. Table layout was garbled in text extraction, so cells were matched by position and by the paper's prose.
agent_relevance: VoT is a text grid, so it is a symbolic code laid out spatially, not a true image. It fits O6 as a spatial-form text.

source: Wu et al. (2024) VoT (quality of the visualization)
finding: The drawn states are often wrong, and right answers depend on right drawings.
numbers: State visualization accurate only about 24-26%; rule compliance about 51-52%; correct decisions in 65-77% of cases when the state drawing was accurate.
limits: One model (GPT-4); no test of whether wrong drawings cause wrong answers or follow from them.
agent_relevance: Drawn states need a code check. An unchecked sketch is a source of errors.

source: Wu et al. (2024) VoT (boundary conditions)
finding: VoT fails where text reasoning is easier: on a ring (clock arithmetic) task GPT-4 CoT beats VoT. Wording matters: dropping the word 'reasoning' raised tracking. Weaker models gain little.
numbers: Ring size 12, 200 items: CoT 52.5% vs VoT 49.5%. Tracking rate in tiling: 87.1% VoT vs 57.4% CoT. Route planning: dropping 'reasoning' raised tracking 78.5 points to 98.5% and accuracy 3.5 points to 62.5%. LLAMA3-8B tiling VoT 46.73 vs CoT 47.24; LLAMA3-70B 56.03 vs 56.41; GPT-3.5 navigation 16.50 vs 9.00.
limits: Single prompt wording tested; no repeats reported in text read.
agent_relevance: Visualization is not free: use it for spatial state tracking, skip it for modular arithmetic. A model-capacity threshold applies.

source: Li et al. (2025) Imagine while reasoning in space: Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought (MVoT)
finding: A fine-tuned model that generates images as thoughts matches or beats text CoT, mainly where text coordinates break down.
numbers: Anole 7B. Maze 92.95% and MiniBehavior 95.14% (CoT above 95% on both). FrozenLake 85.60%, higher than CoT. 90.80% of CoT errors on FrozenLake come from wrong hole coordinates. As a plug-in to GPT-4o: over +15 points on all three tasks.
limits: On two of three tasks text CoT is as good or better. Fine-tuned on task data. Image fidelity errors seen in FrozenLake backgrounds.
agent_relevance: Pictorial codes help most when the scene has many entities, because text coordinates get lost. Needs training, so not a prompt-only move.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Visual Sketchpad: sketching as a visual chain of thought for multimodal language models
finding: Letting a multimodal model draw (code-made plots, auxiliary lines) raises accuracy on math and vision tasks.
numbers: Math tasks: average +11.2% for GPT-4o and +23.4% for GPT-4 Turbo. GPT-4o maxflow 25.0 to 66.3 (+41.3). Vision tasks: +14.3% (GPT-4o) and +18.5% (GPT-4 Turbo). Humans draw the same auxiliary line as GPT-4o in 80% of geometry problems; raters judged GPT-4o plans valid in 92.8%.
limits: Drawing is code-made, so part of the gain is tool use and exact computation, not imagery. One cell in Table 1 is negative (-9.0, parity, a baseline model).
agent_relevance: The sketch is an external, checkable tool output, which matches the program-decides design better than free imagery.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Machine Mental Imagery (Mirage): latent visual tokens
finding: Hidden visual-like tokens interleaved with text give small gains over text-only fine-tuning and beat image-generating models.
numbers: Qwen2.5-VL 7B, 1,000 training samples. VSP spatial reasoning avg 0.86 (direct) and 0.87 (CoT) vs CoT SFT 0.84; with GRPO 0.89 vs 0.85. Spatial planning 0.76 (direct) and 0.58 (CoT) vs direct SFT 0.72 and CoT SFT 0.47. MVoT reproduction 0.61 and 0.11; Anole 0.52 and 0.01. SAT real 0.72 vs 0.66.
limits: Gain over direct SFT is 3 points on reasoning. On planning, thoughts hurt (CoT SFT 0.47 vs direct 0.72). MVoT reproduction was below its published number.
agent_relevance: Weak, mixed support. Needs training, so not usable in a prompt-only scaffold.

source: Synthesis from opened sources: what discriminates the two sides
finding: Response times fit both accounts. Brain data (V1 retinotopy, decoding, TMS) are the best discriminators the depictive side offers; the descriptive side still holds these are not proof of a functional picture. Aphantasia adds a second discriminator: people with no reported images still do spatial tasks.
numbers: No pooled effect size or meta-analysis was found in the opened sources. Rotation test at ceiling (over 90%) in all three groups of Milton 2021.
limits: This is the agent's own synthesis of b01, b10 and b13.
agent_relevance: Practical answer for the agent: two codes exist, so choose per task by testing, not by argument.
